An HTML report often needs one interactive figure for both hemispheres and
several result maps. Repeating a widget for every map wastes space and sends
the same mesh to the browser many times. `surface_scene()` describes the
geometries, maps, labels, and fallback once; `surfwidget()` displays that scene
in R Markdown or Quarto; and `write_surface_scene()` writes the same scene as
an ordinary web page.

This article builds one bilateral viewer with two selectable maps. The example
uses package data, runs without a network connection, and keeps the scientific
transformation in R.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
Sys.setenv(RGL_USE_NULL = "TRUE")
options(rgl.useNULL = TRUE)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  out.width = "100%",
  fig.height = 6
)

library(neurosurf)
```

```{r albers-classes, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
cat(sprintf(
  paste0(
    '<script>document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded",function(){',
    'document.body.classList.remove("palette-red","palette-lapis","palette-ochre","palette-teal","palette-green","palette-violet","preset-homage","preset-interaction","preset-study","preset-structural","preset-adobe","preset-midnight");',
    'document.body.classList.add("palette-%s","preset-%s");',
    '});</script>'
  ),
  params$family,
  params$preset
))
```

## What does a scene contain?

A `SurfaceScene` has one `SurfaceGeometry` per hemisphere and one or more named
scalar layers. Each bilateral layer supplies a left and right value vector
whose lengths match the corresponding geometry. A scene also records the
initial map, legend metadata, provenance, alternative text, and fallback text.

The example uses the fsaverage5 template bundled with neurosurf: inflated
surfaces for display, white surfaces to place the example clusters, and
sulcal depth for the grey anatomy underneath the maps.

```{r load-geometries}
inflated <- load_fsaverage("fsaverage5", "inflated")
white <- load_fsaverage("fsaverage5", "white")
sulc <- load_fsaverage_sulc("fsaverage5")

# Display anatomy, lighter on gyri. FreeSurfer sulc is positive in
# sulci, so it is negated. The report preset's grey ramp saturates at
# |0.1|; scaling to that range keeps a quiet, continuous ramp instead
# of a hard two-tone.
anatomy <- list(
  left = 0.2 * normalize_surface_anatomy(-sulc$lh, "continuous"),
  right = 0.2 * normalize_surface_anatomy(-sulc$rh, "continuous")
)
```

The browser renders the values that R supplies. Perform thresholding, capping,
atlas projection, and other scientific transformations before constructing a
layer. Here two synthetic *z* maps are built from smooth clusters placed at
white-surface coordinates and falling off with distance over the inflated
surface:

```{r prepare-maps}
cluster <- function(hemi, centre, peak, width = 12) {
  seed <- which.min(colSums((t(coords(white[[hemi]])) - centre)^2))
  xyz <- coords(inflated[[hemi]])
  peak * exp(-colSums((t(xyz) - xyz[seed, ])^2) / (2 * width^2))
}
contrast <- function(centres, lh_peaks, rh_peaks) {
  one_side <- function(hemi, side, peaks) {
    Reduce(`+`, Map(function(centre, peak) {
      cluster(hemi, centre * c(side, 1, 1), peak)
    }, centres, peaks))
  }
  list(left = one_side("lh", -1, lh_peaks),
       right = one_side("rh", 1, rh_peaks))
}

memory <- contrast(
  centres = list(c(45, -60, 20), c(40, 20, 30), c(55, -20, 0)),
  lh_peaks = c(4, 3, -3.5), rh_peaks = c(3.5, 2.5, -2.8)
)
# A right-hand movement: left motor cortex dominates
motor <- contrast(
  centres = list(c(38, -22, 56), c(10, -60, 50)),
  lh_peaks = c(4.5, -3), rh_peaks = c(-2.2, -3)
)
```

A binary region of interest, used below as a reference layer: every vertex
within 18 mm of a point in the intraparietal sulcus, again measured over the
inflated surface.

```{r prepare-regions}
roi <- function(hemi, centre, radius = 18) {
  seed <- which.min(colSums((t(coords(white[[hemi]])) - centre)^2))
  xyz <- coords(inflated[[hemi]])
  as.numeric(colSums((t(xyz) - xyz[seed, ])^2) < radius^2)
}
region <- list(left = roi("lh", c(-30, -55, 45)),
               right = roi("rh", c(30, -55, 45)))
```

```{r validate-inputs, include=FALSE}
stopifnot(
  length(memory$left) == nrow(coords(inflated$lh)),
  length(memory$right) == nrow(coords(inflated$rh)),
  any(memory$left > 2),
  any(memory$left < -2),
  any(abs(motor$right) > 2),
  sum(region$left) > 20,
  all(region$left %in% c(0, 1)),
  all(region$right %in% c(0, 1))
)
```

## How do you build one bilateral, multi-map viewer?

Create each named map with `surface_layer()`, then put both geometries and all
layers in one scene. `selected_layer` chooses the map shown when the viewer
opens.

For thresholded two-sided maps, use a palette whose tails start at clearly
visible colours and never pass through the light anatomy grey: blue for
negative, red for positive. `surface_palette()` with the same limits and
threshold returns exactly the colours `surface_figure()` would use, so the
interactive and static figures agree. The layer's `threshold` hides
|*z*| < 2 and marks the gap in the colour key; `magnitude_opacity` fades
colour in between |*z*| = 2 and 2.6, so cluster edges are smooth instead of
following the mesh's triangles. Unthresholded values are passed in, and
`NA` is kept for genuinely missing data.

```{r build-scene}
z_colors <- surface_palette("two_sided", limits = c(-5, 5),
                            threshold = 2)
z_layer <- function(name, values, title) {
  surface_layer(name, values, colormap = z_colors, limits = c(-5, 5),
                threshold = c(-2, 2), units = "z",
                magnitude_opacity = list(low = 2, high = 2.6),
                legend = list(title = title))
}

scene <- surface_scene(
  left = inflated$lh,
  right = inflated$rh,
  curvature = anatomy,
  layers = list(
    z_layer("memory", memory, "Memory contrast"),
    z_layer("motor", motor, "Motor contrast")
  ),
  selected_layer = "memory",
  metadata = list(template = "fsaverage5"),
  provenance = list(source = "synthetic clusters on package data"),
  fallback = "Inflated cortical surfaces with two thresholded z maps.",
  alt_text = paste(
    "Inflated left and right cortical surfaces showing a selectable",
    "thresholded z map, blue negative and red positive, |z| above 2."
  ),
  preset = "report",
  mode = "report"
)
```

```{r validate-scene, include=FALSE}
stopifnot(
  methods::is(scene, "SurfaceScene"),
  identical(names(scene@geometries), c("left", "right")),
  identical(names(scene@layers), c("memory", "motor")),
  identical(scene@selected_layer, "memory")
)
```

Pass the scene to `surfwidget()` once. The map selector changes the active
values and legend without constructing another widget or another WebGL
context.

```{r render-scene}
surfwidget(scene, width = "100%", height = "420px")
```

The report toolbar provides the authored map selector, coordinated anatomical
views, reset, and PNG export. Drag to rotate, use the wheel or a pinch gesture
to zoom, and right-drag to pan.

## How do you keep a reference region beneath the selected effect map?

Give one binary layer `role = "reference"` and an explicit color. It has its
own checkbox, opacity slider and categorical swatch. It stays beneath either
quantitative map and cannot become the selected map or enter effect readouts.
Reset restores its authored visibility and opacity.

```{r reference-scene}
reference_scene <- surface_scene(
  left = inflated$lh, right = inflated$rh,
  layers = c(scene@layers, list(surface_layer(
    "reference", region, role = "reference", color = "#238b45",
    opacity = 0.4, legend = list(title = "Intraparietal ROI"),
    provenance = list(source = "synthetic 18 mm disc")
  ))),
  curvature = anatomy,
  preset = "report",
  fallback = "Bilateral z maps over a faint intraparietal ROI.",
  alt_text = "Thresholded z maps over a green intraparietal region."
)
stopifnot(identical(reference_scene@selected_layer, "memory"))
```

```{r show-reference-scene}
surfwidget(reference_scene, width = "100%", height = "360px")
```

The green region sits beneath whichever map is selected and keeps its own
swatch, checkbox and opacity slider; it never enters the colour key.
References require a full 0/1 mask per hemisphere, with no limits, units,
indices or thresholds.

The CPU renderer draws the same membership beneath a static map, in the
order anatomy, reference, effect:

```{r static-reference}
image <- render_surface_rgba(
  inflated$lh, memory$left, anatomy_metric = sulc$lh,
  threshold = 2, limits = c(-5, 5), alpha_ramp = 0.6,
  reference = list(
    id = "reference", label = "Intraparietal ROI",
    mask = region$left, color = "#238b45", opacity = 0.4
  ),
  width = 600, height = 380, antialias = 2
)
```

```{r static-reference-image, echo=FALSE, out.width="75%", fig.align="center", fig.cap="Left hemisphere, lateral view: the intraparietal ROI (green, 40% opacity) beneath the memory *z* map (|*z*| &gt; 2, limits &plusmn;5)."}
file <- knitr::fig_path("reference.png")
dir.create(dirname(file), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
write_surface_rgba(image, file)
knitr::include_graphics(file)
```

Both renderers classify membership at 0.5 after linear interpolation, and
triangles outside the cortex mask never receive reference colour. A static
figure should label the reference with its own swatch, outside the effect
colour scale; `tools/reference-specimen.R` is a complete example.

Supply already projected binary membership. For a volume label, use explicit
categorical/nearest-voxel sampling and record the source and mesh identity,
depth aggregation and projection parameters in `provenance`. This API does
not perform projection or inference.

## Which option controls appearance and behavior?

`preset` sets appearance and `mode` sets behaviour; the scene above uses
`preset = "report"` with `mode = "report"`.

| Setting | Controls | What it changes |
|---|---|---|
| `preset = "report"` | Appearance | Two-tone sulcal greys on a neutral grey panel, lit for on-screen reading; made for report widgets. |
| `preset = "paper-light"` | Appearance | White background, stronger folding contrast, and print-oriented PNG defaults. |
| `mode = "report"` | Behavior | Lazy mounting, the compact report toolbar, deterministic initial framing, and fallback/print behavior. |
| `mode = "viewer"` | Behavior | A bare rotatable viewer without the report toolbar. |

Tweakpane is deprecated. The report runtime does not load it or contact a CDN.
Legacy `showControls` and `controlType` configuration entries warn during the
migration; use the scene `mode` instead.

## How is geometry shared across maps?

`surface_scene_manifest()` converts numeric arrays to typed binary assets and
addresses each asset by its SHA-256 digest. The scene refers to each hemisphere
geometry once. Each additional full bilateral map contributes two value
arrays, not another copy of the vertices or faces.

```{r inspect-assets}
manifest <- surface_scene_manifest(scene, asset_mode = "inline")
roles <- vapply(manifest$assets, `[[`, character(1), "role")
bytes <- vapply(manifest$assets, `[[`, numeric(1), "byteLength")

data.frame(
  content = c("geometry", "map values"),
  assets = c(sum(roles %in% c("vertices", "faces", "curvature")),
             sum(roles == "values")),
  bytes = c(sum(bytes[roles %in% c("vertices", "faces", "curvature")]),
            sum(bytes[roles == "values"]))
)
```

```{r validate-assets, include=FALSE}
stopifnot(
  length(manifest$geometries) == 2L,
  length(manifest$layers) == 2L,
  sum(roles == "vertices") == 2L,
  sum(roles == "values") == 4L
)
```

Missing map values remain IEEE `NaN` values in the binary payload. The browser
verifies every adjacent asset's byte length and checksum before constructing
the scene.

## How do you write an offline report?

Use `write_surface_scene()` when the viewer must live outside an R Markdown or
Quarto document. Both output modes bundle the compatible surfviewjs runtime
locally and make no network requests.

```{r write-reports, eval=FALSE}
# index.html, the runtime, and content-addressed .bin files
write_surface_scene(scene, "surface-report", self_contained = FALSE)

# one index.html with the runtime and typed arrays inlined
write_surface_scene(scene, "surface-report-inline",
                    self_contained = TRUE)
```

Choose adjacent assets for a site or a report directory: the browser can cache
the runtime and SHA-addressed arrays, and repeated assets are deduplicated.
Choose a self-contained file when a single portable HTML file matters more than
file size or cross-page caching.

```{r validate-report-writers, include=FALSE}
adjacent_dir <- tempfile("neurosurf-adjacent-")
inline_dir <- tempfile("neurosurf-inline-")
adjacent_html <- write_surface_scene(
  scene, adjacent_dir, self_contained = FALSE
)
inline_html <- write_surface_scene(scene, inline_dir, self_contained = TRUE)
stopifnot(
  file.exists(adjacent_html),
  file.exists(inline_html),
  file.exists(file.path(adjacent_dir, "surfview.embed.iife.js")),
  length(list.files(adjacent_dir, pattern = "\\.bin$")) > 0L
)
```

## How do you mount the scene on a plain web page?

The HTML writer produces a minimal page that uses the public
`surfview.mountSurfView()` API. You can customize its generated `index.html` or
use the same lifecycle in another page. In this example, `manifest` is a
`surfview.scene.v1` object produced by `surface_scene_manifest()`:

```html
<div id="surface-report"></div>
<script src="./surfview.embed.iife.js"></script>
<script>
  const handle = surfview.mountSurfView(
    document.getElementById("surface-report"),
    manifest,
    {
      lazy: true,
      preset: "paper-light",
      controls: true,
      baseUrl: document.baseURI,
      bilateralGroup: {
        id: "bilateral",
        leftSurfaceId: "left",
        rightSurfaceId: "right"
      }
    }
  );

  handle.ready.then(() => handle.setView("lateral"));
  window.addEventListener("pagehide", () => handle.dispose(), { once: true });
</script>
```

A manifest with both hemispheres must name a `bilateralGroup` that pairs the
left and right surface ids; without it the report runtime refuses to mount.
`surfwidget()` and `write_surface_scene()` supply this option automatically.

The returned handle also provides `selectLayer()`, `resize()`, `exportPNG()`,
and `dispose()`. Call `dispose()` when an application removes or replaces the
viewer so it can release observers, listeners, animation frames, the WebGL
context, and GPU resources.

## What happens when interaction is unavailable?

`fallback` is required plain text. The widget and standalone writer expose it
when JavaScript is disabled or WebGL initialization fails, and print CSS shows
it instead of a blank canvas. `alt_text` labels the interactive figure for
assistive technology.

The fallback text is not a bitmap renderer. If a report needs a visual print,
PDF, or archival representation, build a static figure from the same R values
with `surface_figure()`; see `vignette("surface-figures")`.

## When should you use the legacy shortcuts?

`surfwidget()` still accepts `SurfaceGeometry`, `NeuroSurface`,
`ColorMappedNeuroSurface`, and `VertexColoredNeuroSurface`. Those methods adapt
a single surface to a `SurfaceScene` and are useful for quick exploration:

```{r legacy-shortcut, eval=FALSE}
surface <- NeuroSurface(inflated$lh, nodes(inflated$lh), memory$left)
surfwidget(surface, irange = c(-5, 5))
```

Use an explicit `SurfaceScene` for bilateral figures, multiple named maps,
portable assets, authored fallback text, provenance, or report behavior.
